A Variational Inequality Perspective on Generative Adversarial Nets

Stability has been a recurrent issue in training generative adversarial networks (GANs). One common way to tackle this issue has been to propose new formulations of the GAN objective. Yet, surprisingly few studies have looked at optimization methods specifically designed for this adversarial training. In this work, we review the “variational inequality” framework which contains most formulations of the GAN objective introduced so far. Taping into the mathematical programming literature, we counter some common misconceptions about the difficulties of saddle point optimization and propose to extend standard methods designed for variational inequalities to GANs training, such as a stochastic version of the extragradient method, and empirically investigate their behavior on GANs.
1 Introduction

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) (Goodfellow et al., 2014) form an approach to generative modeling known for producing appealing samples such as for image generation. Nevertheless, GANs are also known to be hard to train, often displaying an unstable behavior. Much recent research has been devoted to try to stabilize the training of GANs. One common way to tackle this issue has been to propose new formulations of the GAN objective (Nowozin et al., 2016; Arjovsky et al., 2017).

In this work, we opt instead to leverage standard techniques coming from the mathematical programming literature. In particular, we point out that most GAN settings proposed so far can be cast as a variational inequality problem (Harker and Pang, 1990), which is also the general framework within which saddle point optimization algorithms were developed (Korpelevich, 1976). Consequently, we propose to tap into this literature and apply its standard methods to train GANs. We will also show that some of the issues of GAN training noticed so far can be explained with standard variational inequality optimization results. Moreover, we introduce a novel setting able to handle the non-boundedness of the model parameters and the non-convexity of the cost functions (by only assuming local convexity), which are non-standard assumptions in the variational inequality literature.

Contributions. We introduce for the first time an analysis of GANs objectives within the framework of variational inequality, well-known in optimization. We bring from the related literature standard methods and results to solve variational inequalities, namely averaging the iterates as well as the extragradient method. We extend their analysis to the specificity of GANs training, namely stochasticity, non-boundedness and local convexity. Finally, we provide experimental evidence on the ability of these methods to stabilize GANs training.

This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the background on GANs and on optimization. Section 3 explains how to cast the optimization problem of GANs as a variational inequality and reviews the framework. Section 4 introduces the standard methods to optimize variational inequalities and Section 5 presents the experimental results.

The minimax formulation is theoretically convenient because a large literature on games studies this problem and provides guaranties on the existence of equilibria. One important point to notice is that the two optimization problems in (3) are coupled and have to be considered jointly from an optimization point of view. On the other hand, standard GANs are non-convex (i.e. each cost function is non-convex), and thus such equilibria may not exist, bringing optimization issues. In particular, when no equilibrium exists, following the gradient may be unstable and lead to iterates with a constantly growing norm. Even if an equilibrium point does exist, a bad initialization may lead to the same unwanted behavior.

Proving the existence of an equilibrium in GANs is outside the scope of this work. Instead in the following we focus on ways to optimize these games assuming that an equilibrium exists. As is often standard in non-convex optimization, we will also focus on finding points satisfying the necessary stationary conditions (though which are not automatically sufficient unless there is some local convexity). Fortunately, the optimization literature has studied for a long time what is called variational inequality problems which generalizes the stationary conditions for two player games problems. 6 Related Work

Now that we have introduced a more general framework optimizing in GANs, we can look at the previous work thought the prism of the variational inequality literature. The extragradient method is the standard algorithm to optimize variational inequalities. This algorithm has been originally introduced by Korpelevich (1976) and extended by Nesterov (2007) and Nemirovski (2004). Stochastic versions of the extragradient have been recently analyzed (Juditsky et al., 2011; Yousefian et al., 2014; Iusem et al., 2017) in the context of stochastic variational inequalities with bounded constraints. A linearly convergent variance reduced version of the stochastic gradient method has been proposed by Palaniappan and Bach (2016) for strongly monotone variational inequalities.

A first idea to optimize the two-players game (3) is to sequentially fully optimize the discriminator for a fixed generator, then make a gradient step for this “optimal” discriminator, and repeat this process. This way of optimizing (3) can be related with (Arjovsky et al., 2017) where several updates ( [MATH n_{\text{critic}}=5] ncritic=5n_{\text{critic}}=5 in practice) are processed on the discriminator between each update of the generator. It is also the case in (Metz et al., 2017) where they explicitly try to construct the “true generator objective function” unrolling for [MATH K] KK steps. Nevertheless the fact that this “true generator function” cannot be found with a satisfying accuracy may lead to a different behavior that the one expected.

Several methods to stabilize GANs consist in transforming the minimax formulation (SP) into a more general variational inequality that can no longer be cast as a saddle point problem. This is the case of the non-saturating formulation of GANs (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Fedus et al., 2017), the DCGANs (Radford et al., 2016), the gradient penalty55 5 (Gulrajani et al., 2017, Eq.(3)) is a bit confusing but one can notice that in their Alg. 1 the gradient penalty is only added to the discriminator cost function. Since this gradient penalty depends also on the generator, WGAN-GP cannot be cast as a SP problem. for WGANs (Gulrajani et al., 2017). Yadav et al. (2018) propose an optimization method for GANs based on AltSGD using a momentum based extrapolation step on the generator. Mescheder et al. (2017) propose to add the norm of the gradient in the objective and provide an interesting perspective on GANs, interpreting the training as the research of a two-players game equilibrium. A study of the continuous version of two player games has been done by Ratliff et al. (2016) and interesting non-convex results have been proved in the context of GANs by Grnarova et al. (2018).
7 Conclusion

We have presented a new framework called variational inequality to consider GAN objectives. We tapped into the optimization literature to bring new techniques to train GANs and provided empirical as well as theoretical evidence on the benefits of averaging and extrapolation steps. On one hand, the former seems to improve the inception score at convergence, on the other hand the latter looks to be more stable for step size tuning. Nevertheless, we just considered two standard algorithms. We have just scratched the surface and hope it opens the door to a new algorithmic perspective on training GANs.
